chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Hal McIntyre and the freelance arrangers of New York
summary: Horace wrote a couple of charts for Hal McIntyre's upstate nightclub band, and describes freelancers like Fred Norman and Andy Gibson who solicited bandleaders needing weekly broadcast arrangements.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Hal McIntyre. I did a couple of things for him, not many. He was playing upstate New York in a fabulous nightclub, if I remember correctly. And, you know, he played good sax, he did -- brilliant tone and whatnot. But he wanted -- he didn't want the wild stuff, if I remember correctly. He wanted something, because of the type of exclusive engagements that he played, he wanted something that was not too far out, but yet it had a beat -- I remember him from this, you know. So I made a couple of things for him.

You know, in New York there were quite a few guys during that era, like there was a great arranger named Fred Norman. He was in Claude Hopkins' band, and he was a trombonist and he wrote real good, you know, and -- oh, a guy named Andy Gibson. He was with Charlie Barnett. We were in there together. Now he wrote a lot of things. And -- I'm mentioning these things to say that in those days they had a lot of free lance arrangers, you know, and we used to -- in that thing when I say we, because I was scuffling at that bit too at that time -- and we used to go around and listen at bands, and then we would solicit, see, you know, our writing, you know, the different bandleaders and say, 'Well, I'm an arranger, you know, and go up and meet them.'
Naturally, during those days -- especially when the

bands were broadcasting, they had to have arrangements, and they had to have tunes, so naturally they were interested in, you know, getting as many arrangements as possible, because they had to send their programs in a week at a time to broadcast, so they had to be clear, one of those things.
So this is what the arrangers found out, and naturally we would take advantage of that, you know. This is how we got to do something. So if you do a good job, you --
Yeah, the word would get around.
You'd get more work. --(unintelligible) Yeah, the word would get around, for sure. So this is what happened with Hal McIntyre.

See, he was a nice guy. And it was in those days easy to write for his band because it was, you know, everybody read. He wanted you to bear in mind, just like I said before, it couldn't be too far out, but he did want something with a beat. That was it.
